title: Demonstrate understanding of employment relations in an organisation

lessons.title: The employment relationship and the law
lessons.html:
What are employment relations?

Employment relations is the relationship between the employer, the employees and, where they exist, the trade unions. When this relationship is good, people work well together, conflict is handled fairly and the business runs smoothly. When it is poor, there can be grievances, disputes, absenteeism and even strikes.

The employment contract

Every employee should have a written contract or written particulars of employment. It sets out the job title, hours, pay, leave, notice period and other conditions. Both sides have duties:

  • Employer: pay on time, provide a safe workplace, treat workers fairly, follow labour law.
  • Employee: do the work properly, follow reasonable instructions, be on time, follow rules and act honestly.

Key South African labour laws

LawMain purpose
Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995Fair dismissal, unions, collective bargaining, dispute resolution, strikes
Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997Minimum conditions: working hours, overtime, leave, notice
Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998No unfair discrimination; fair representation in the workplace
Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993Safe and healthy workplace

Agriculture also has sectoral determinations and the national minimum wage, which set minimum pay. Your HR office can tell you the current rates. As a supervisor you do not need to know every detail, but you must know that these laws exist and where to get advice.

The supervisor's role

On the abattoir floor, the supervisor is often the face of management. How you treat people affects the whole relationship. Be consistent, fair and respectful, apply rules the same way to everyone and communicate clearly.

lessons.title: Grievances, discipline and unions
lessons.html:
Handling problems fairly

Grievances

A grievance is a complaint by an employee about how they have been treated at work, for example unfair allocation of overtime, a problem with a co-worker or a safety concern. Most organisations have a written grievance procedure:

  1. The employee raises the grievance with the direct supervisor, usually within a set time.
  2. The supervisor listens, investigates and tries to resolve it.
  3. If not resolved, it goes to the next level of management.
  4. Outcomes are recorded in writing.

Take every grievance seriously. Unresolved grievances grow into bigger disputes.

Discipline

Discipline is meant to correct behaviour, not to punish. A disciplinary code lists offences and usual sanctions. Progressive discipline means steps increase if behaviour continues: verbal warning, written warning, final written warning, and then possibly dismissal. Very serious offences, like theft or assault, may lead to dismissal for a first offence after a fair hearing.

For discipline to be fair, there must be a valid reason and a fair procedure. The employee must know the rule, be told of the allegations, be given a chance to respond and be allowed representation according to the code. Keep accurate records.

Trade unions and workplace forums

Employees have the right to join a trade union. Unions represent members in grievances, disciplinary hearings and wage negotiations. Shop stewards are elected worker representatives on site. A good supervisor builds a respectful working relationship with shop stewards and does not victimise anyone for union membership.

Disputes and the CCMA

If a dispute cannot be resolved inside the organisation, it can be referred to the Commission for Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration (CCMA) or a bargaining council. The CCMA first tries to help the parties agree (conciliation) and, if that fails, may decide the matter (arbitration).

lessons.title: Building good working relationships
lessons.html:
Preventing conflict

The best employment relations come from everyday good practice, not from procedures alone.

Communication

  • Hold short daily or weekly team meetings to share production targets, safety matters and changes.
  • Explain the reasons for decisions, such as why the shift times change in the festive season.
  • Listen to concerns and give feedback on what was done.
  • Put important information on the notice board and, where needed, explain it in the languages your team understands.

Fairness and consistency

Workers notice when rules are applied to some but not others. Allocate overtime, leave and tasks fairly. Do not show favouritism to friends or family. Never discriminate on grounds such as race, gender, religion, HIV status, disability or language.

Recognition

Thank people for good work. Recognise a team that met its target with zero injuries. Small acts of recognition improve morale.

Handling conflict between workers

  1. Act early before it grows.
  2. Speak to each person privately.
  3. Bring them together to find a solution they both accept.
  4. Focus on behaviour and work, not personalities.
  5. Follow up later to check it is resolved.

Knowing your limits

A supervisor should know when to involve HR or senior management, for example in cases of serious misconduct, harassment, possible dismissal or union disputes. Getting advice early protects both the employee and the organisation.

Key points

  • Employment relations involve employer, employees and unions.
  • Key laws include the Labour Relations Act, the Basic Conditions of Employment Act and the Employment Equity Act.
  • Grievances must be heard and resolved through a fair procedure.
  • Fair discipline needs a valid reason and a fair procedure.
  • Unresolved disputes may go to the CCMA or a bargaining council.
  • Consistent, fair and respectful supervision prevents conflict.
